questions.solution_text:
Let $\theta=\arctan x$. When $x>0$, $\theta$ lies in $\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, so $\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta$ is also in the range of $\arctan$ and $\arctan\frac{1}{x}=\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta$.
The sum is then $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
When $x<0$ both terms are negative, so the sum is $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ instead.
The identity holds exactly when $x>0$.

questions.question_text:
A proof of $\arccos x+\arcsin x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ begins: let $\theta=\arcsin x$, so $\sin\theta=x$ with $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}$.
Which statement correctly completes the next line of the proof?

options.text: $\cos\theta=x$, so $\arccos x=\theta$ and the two inverse functions are equal.
options.why: Confuses the two ratios: $\theta$ was defined so that $\sin\theta=x$, not $\cos\theta=x$.
Uses the wrong co-ratio: $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)$ equals $\cos\theta$, not $x$.
Uses the supplementary identity, but $\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\theta$, which is not $x$.
